recipe.history:
Spinach — Spinacia oleracea — is a flowering plant in the family Amaranthaceae, originating in ancient Persia (modern-day Iran and surrounding regions), where it was cultivated and eaten as far back as the fourth century CE. Arab traders carried it westward along the Silk Road, and by the eleventh century it had spread to Spain through the Moorish occupation, becoming a prized vegetable in Andalusian cooking. The medieval Arab culinary world embraced spinach enthusiastically — a tenth-century Arabic agricultural text from Andalusia, the Kitab al-Filaha, describes multiple preparations for the vegetable. By the twelfth and thirteenth centuries, spinach had reached France and England, where it was often referred to as 'the prince of vegetables' in monastic writing. Catherine de' Medici, who married the future King Henry II of France in 1533, reportedly loved spinach so much that she requested it at every meal, inspiring the French culinary term 'à la Florentine' to describe any dish that includes spinach — a term still in use today in professional kitchens. The vegetable's iron and mineral content was long exaggerated in popular culture (the Popeye cartoons of the 1930s attributed spinach's iron levels to a decimal-point error in an 1870 German study), but its genuine nutritional density and culinary versatility have kept it central to cuisines across Europe, the Middle East, South Asia, and America.

Creamed spinach arrived in American fine dining through the steakhouse tradition of the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, where it became a canonical side dish — particularly in New York steakhouses like Peter Luger, where it is served in cast iron alongside thick porterhouses. The dish's richness — spinach wilted into submission and then folded through a béchamel or cream sauce enriched with butter and Parmesan — made it a natural companion for beef, its vegetable heartiness cutting through the fat of the steak without ever becoming prim or virtuous. The idea of putting creamed spinach on a burger — bringing the steakhouse side dish onto the patty itself — is an act of logical compression: if creamed spinach belongs next to a steak, why not under the top bun? The NICE GUYS SPINACH LAST BURGER takes this logic seriously, piling the burger high with silky, Parmesan-enriched creamed spinach that drapes over the patty like a savory blanket.

I have a very specific memory of the first time I ordered creamed spinach at a New York steakhouse — a place with red leather booths and waiters who had been there for thirty years and called everyone 'hon.' The creamed spinach arrived in a small cast-iron crock, deep green and glossy, rich with cream and nutmeg and a sharp edge of Parmesan. I ate half of it with a spoon before the steak even arrived and felt no shame whatsoever. Years later, I was making burgers on a weeknight and had leftover creamed spinach in the refrigerator from the night before. I reheated it in a small pan, added an extra grating of Parmesan, and spooned it lavishly over a freshly cooked medium-rare patty. It was everything I remembered from that steakhouse, compressed into a burger, on a Tuesday. Sometimes weeknight cooking does something that a fine dining establishment cannot: it gives you exactly what you want, exactly when you want it, with no ceremony and no waiting.

The philosophy of medium rare — 130 to 135 degrees Fahrenheit — is especially apt when creamed spinach is involved. The sauce is rich, fatty, and warming; without a juicy, assertive, pink-centered patty beneath it, the whole thing risks becoming a pile of cream and spinach on a bun with nothing to anchor it. The medium-rare patty provides that anchor: its seared crust gives structural contrast to the soft, creamy spinach; its juicy interior provides the beefy backbone that the entire dish rests on. Cooking the patty further would produce a dry, compact disk that disappears beneath the topping. At 130–135°F, the beef earns its place and the creamed spinach earns its glorious excess.
ingredients: 450g fresh baby spinach (or 2 bunches regular spinach, tough stems removed)
kosher salt and white pepper to taste
For the Parmesan crust (optional but recommended):
instructions: 1. Make the buns: Whisk warm milk, sugar, and yeast; rest 5 minutes until foamy. Add butter and egg; mix. Add flour and salt; knead 8–10 minutes. Rise in an oiled bowl 1 hour. Divide into 4 balls, flatten slightly, proof on parchment 30–40 minutes. Brush with egg wash. Bake at 375°F (190°C) for 15–18 minutes until deep golden. Cool on rack.

2. Wilt the spinach: Bring a large pot of salted water to a boil. Blanch spinach for 30 seconds until just wilted. Drain immediately and transfer to an ice bath to stop cooking. Drain again, then squeeze very firmly in a clean kitchen towel to remove as much moisture as possible. Roughly chop the squeezed spinach. Set aside.

3. Make the creamed spinach: Melt butter in a heavy saucepan over medium heat. Add diced onion and cook 5 minutes until softened and translucent. Add minced garlic; cook 60 seconds. Sprinkle in flour and stir constantly for 90 seconds, cooking out the raw flour taste. Gradually whisk in the heavy cream and milk, adding in a slow stream and whisking to prevent lumps. Bring to a gentle simmer, stirring, until sauce thickens, about 4–5 minutes.

4. Stir in the grated Parmesan, nutmeg, and cayenne. Fold in the chopped, squeezed spinach. Stir until the spinach is fully incorporated and the sauce coats it thickly. Season generously with salt and white pepper. Reduce heat to low to keep warm, stirring occasionally.

5. Form the patties: Divide ground beef into 4 equal portions (about 175g each). Form into patties 4 inches wide and 3/4 inch thick, pressing a center dimple. Season both sides with salt, pepper, and garlic powder just before cooking.

6. Cook the patties: Heat a cast-iron skillet over high heat until very hot. Add a thin film of neutral oil. Sear patties without moving for 3 minutes. Flip. Lay a slice of provolone on each patty. Cook 2 more minutes. Target internal temperature: 130–135°F (54–57°C) for medium rare. Rest 3 minutes off heat.

7. Optional Parmesan crust on buns: Sprinkle 1 tablespoon of grated Parmesan on the cut face of each top bun. Press down lightly to adhere. Toast cut-side down in the skillet 60–90 seconds until the Parmesan melts and crisps and the bun is golden. Toast the bottom buns separately without cheese.

8. Assemble: Place the provolone-topped patty on the bottom bun. Spoon a generous, heaping mound of hot creamed spinach directly over the patty — let it be excessive; it should drape over the sides slightly. Add tomato slices and red onion rings. Close with the Parmesan-crusted top bun. Serve immediately while the creamed spinach is hot.
